title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1LC1LB_1LE0LD_1LE1LC_0RF1RA_---1RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1LC1LB_1LE0LD_1LE1LC_0RF1RA_---1RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and it is now an exact arithmetic question. Read the tape as a list of runs of ones. Lean proves that from one visit of the left end to the next the list changes by an explicit map (visit), and that the machine halts from blank tape exactly when the orbit of the list [12, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] under this map reaches a list in which every run is even (halts_iff). The map is a counter growing by 3/2 per epoch whose parities drive a growing stack of slower counters; a halt needs the whole stack used up. An exact simulator ran 260,000 epochs (about 1091568 steps) without a halt, and the depth the head reaches into the stack falls off geometrically, so a halt looks very unlikely; it is not excluded. Lean also proves that no invariant on the parities of the runs (or on the runs mod 4, 8 or 16) can exclude it, and a list with the same stack as the real run but a different counter value halts: a proof would have to follow the 3/2 counter's arithmetic.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The sweep
claims.text: Read as runs of 1s separated by single 0s, with u a run of length 1: [X, 4, u<sup>n+2</sup>, R] becomes [X+6, 4, u<sup>n</sup>, R] in 2X+32 steps, for every X = 2x+2, every n and every tape R.

claims.title: The conversion
claims.text: [2x+8, u<sup>k+2</sup>, R] becomes [6, 4, u<sup>x</sup>, 4, u<sup>k</sup>, R] in 4x+74 steps: the long run is turned into half as many units.

claims.title: A halt can only happen past the right end
claims.text: A closed tape language from windows of 4 cells covers the run from blank tape; in it the halting transition F0 can only fire with blank tape from the head on, so the machine halts iff F steps onto the blank region right of the tape. The right end of the tape has not moved since step 1.8·10<sup>5</sup>.

claims.title: The moves of one visit
claims.text: Eight shift rules, each for all values of its counts and all tapes around: the entry, E crossing even runs, E meeting an odd run (joined with the next one, or turned into units if it is the last), the halt when E meets two 0s, an even run crumbling into units, the run before it absorbing two of them, and the conversion at the left end.

claims.title: The visit map
claims.text: For every list l of the domain D (runs ≥ 1, none of length 2, first run even and ≥ 12 or the list starting 6, 4, 1, 1): from the visit with runs l the machine reaches the visit with runs visit l, which is again in D, or halts if visit l = none. And visit l = none exactly when all runs (the first after adding 2) are even.

claims.title: Halting is a question about the visit map
claims.text: The run from blank tape is at the visit [12, 19] after 423 steps, so the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of that list under visit reaches none. (Axioms: propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice.)

claims.title: No invariant on run parities, or on runs mod 4, 8 or 16
claims.text: No set of parity words (the list of r mod 2 over the runs) contains the word of [12, 19], is closed under the visit map on the domain D, and avoids every halting list; the same for residues mod 4, 8 and 16. The proof is an explicit chain of lists of D (14, 18, 20 and 56 lists): the first has the residue word of [12, 19], each is mapped to a list with the residue word of the next, the last halts. Checked by decide. (Axioms: propext, Quot.sound.)

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 60,039 cells have been visited and 56,234 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: 83 epochs, 7·10<sup>29</sup> steps, no halt
claims.text: The macro simulator with proved cycle jumps (tools/py/bbtools/cycles.py, exact step counts) runs to 1030 steps. The unit count m of epoch 83 is 780,830,244,113,908; m' = 3m/2 + d with d in {−2, +1, +4} (m even) or {−1/2, +5/2} (m odd), and an epoch takes 1.500·m2 steps.

claims.title: The visit map against the machine
claims.text: The Python form of the map (and a one-to-one mirror of the Lean definitions) predicts all 5,405 visits of the first 3·107 steps; the run-list simulator it is compared with agrees with a cell-by-cell run at every visit of the first 3·106 steps and with py/epochs.py at epoch 82.

claims.title: The last step before a halt
claims.text: Among all 1,628,875 lists of the domain with at most 6 runs (each at most 13), the next visit halts exactly from [X, 1] and [X, 4, odd, odd, even, …, even]; only [X−6, 3] maps to [X, 1]. And directly from the map: the last run of the orbit (a 1) can only become even at a visit where every run except the last two is even, so a halt needs the cascade to work through the whole stack.

claims.title: 260,000 epochs, about 10<sup>91568</sup> steps, no halt
claims.text: The exact run-list simulator (every step of the machine, the proved sweep applied in bulk, big integers) runs 100,000 epochs in a minute: the step count then has 116,996 bits (about 10<sup>35219</sup>) and the stack 113,485 runs. A 15-minute run of the same program reached 260,000 epochs (304,184 bits). No halt.

claims.title: The stack is touched only near its top
claims.text: In 100,000 epochs the head passed 1 entry of the stack in 73% of the epochs, 2 in 22%, 3 in 4%, 4 in 0.27%, 5 in 0.04%, 6 twice, while the stack gains 0.28 entries per epoch; its size never came back more than 10 entries below an earlier value. If the parities keep behaving like coin flips, the chance that the stack is ever emptied is negligible.

claims.title: A halting list with the real stack
claims.text: For large m the next stack depends only on the stack and the parity of m (py/adversary.py), and m' = (3m + c)/2 with c fixed by the stack and the parity. From the stack 4 u17 4 u3 4 1 of the real visit [6, 4, u368, …] at step 181,429, 247 odd epochs and then one even epoch halt the machine. Solving for m gives m0 = 41155288665286261693662459474261276833979426164594950575389163897113542655 (mod 2248); the exact simulator run from [6, 4, um0, 4, u17, 4, u3, 4, 1] halts after 248 epochs (a step count of 780 bits). So a proof has to see m mod 2248. The breadth-first searches over parities (468,328 stacks to depth 19, a sampled search to depth 40) were too shallow to meet this word.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.493). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: A stack of slower counters
claims.text: The list right of the unit block behaves like nested copies of the top level: its first run grows by 6 and loses a unit at each odd epoch, and is converted into units when they run out; deeper items change exponentially more rarely, and the bottom of the list has been frozen for most of the run. The list grows by about one item per three epochs (29 tokens at epoch 83).

claims.title: Rounds between end events, by remainder class
claims.text: Sample the run whenever the head is in state D reading 1 with only 0s to its left. Read rightwards from the head, the tape is then A U^m B: one long periodic block between two short context words. For each class (A, U, B, m modulo 1 or 2 (the smallest modulus that works for the context)) the next sample is simulated for six values of m and extended as an affine map of m (with a cubic step count). Along the direct run from blank tape to 3·109 steps (59 events) the class map predicts the next event in all 25 rounds it applies to. This is an extrapolation checked by computation, not a proof.

claims.title: 1,742 rounds of the class map without a halt
claims.text: Iterated with exact integers from the event at step 181,384 of the run (A = (empty), U = 10, m = 373, B = 14 (01)18 13 (01)4 13 01): 1,742 rounds without meeting a halting class; m then has 519 bits (about 10312 steps of the machine). 1,742 distinct contexts occur, the longest of 2,729 cells.

claims.title: No halting class among 5,000 contexts
claims.text: Breadth first from the starting context, with every remainder at every context (whether or not the numbers can really produce that sequence of remainders, and only for m large compared with the contexts): 5,000 contexts expanded, 6,526 found, to depth 23. None of them halts; the search is not complete (the set of contexts keeps growing), and it says nothing about a halt that needs a context as long as the block itself.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Exactly: does the orbit of [12, 1<sup>9</sup>] under the visit map ever reach a list whose runs are all even? That needs the whole stack to be used up. The number of even runs stays odd, which does not exclude it. No invariant on the runs mod 2, 4, 8 or 16 can exclude it (proved), and a list with the real stack and another counter value does halt, so a proof must use the arithmetic of the 3/2 counter.

check: cd holdouts/1RB1RE_1LC1LB_1LE0LD_1LE1LC_0RF1RA_---1RA && python3 py/rules.py | diff - lean/Rules.lean && python3 py/visit_rules.py | diff - lean/VisitRules.lean

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now pure arithmetic. Read the tape as a list of numbers (the lengths of its runs of ones): each time the head comes back to the left end, the list has changed by a simple rule, and the machine stops only if every number in the list is ever even at once. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the rule.

facts.text: The machine halts exactly when the list of runs, followed by the proved visit map, becomes all even.
One sweep: the long run grows by 6, the unit block loses 2 (proved for all sizes).
No halt in 260,000 epochs of an exact simulator.
Epochs that reach 1, 2, 3 entries into the stack: deeper is geometrically rarer.

sections.heading: Runs of ones
html: Write the tape as the lengths of its runs of 1s, which are separated by single 0s. A run of length 1 (the cells 10) is a unit, written u. Each time the head comes back to the left end in state B the tape reads
[X, 4, un, L]     a long run X, a run of 4, n units, then a list L of short runs

The head never goes far to the right: it shuttles across X and the first units only. That is why the right end of the tape has not moved since step 180,000.

sections.heading: One visit of the left end, as a rule on a list of numbers
html: Write the tape as the list of its runs of ones, left to right, for instance [12, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] (the tape at step 423). A visit is the moment the head stands, in state B, on the blank cell just left of the tape. Between two visits the head makes one trip into the tape and back, and the list changes like this:

1. The first run grows by 2.
  2. The head runs to the right over the even runs until it meets the first odd run. If there is none, the machine halts past the right end.
  3. The odd run is glued to the run after it (their lengths add, plus 2).
  4. On the way back, the even run just before, of length 2t, crumbles into t runs of length 1 (“units”); the run before that swallows two of them and grows by 4, and is then glued in the same way, so that the run before it crumbles too, and so on to the left end.

Example: [18, 8, 5, 4, …] becomes [24, 1, 1, 11, …]. If the cascade reaches the very first run and that one crumbles, the list restarts as [6, 4, 1, 1, …]: that is the conversion that ends an epoch.

Lean's kernel has checked this rule for every list of the kind the machine produces, and that the machine reaches the list above after 423 steps. So the halting question is exactly: starting from [12, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] and applying the rule over and over, do we ever get a list with only even numbers? Every unit is odd, so all the units of the stack would have to be gone at the same moment.

sections.heading: Eat, grow, convert
html: Sweep (proved in Lean for every size): [X, 4, un+2, R] → [X+6, 4, un, R]. The long run eats two units and grows by six cells.
Conversion (proved too): when the units are gone, [2x+8, uk+2, R] → [6, 4, ux, 4, uk, R]: the long run is turned back into half as many units.

So an epoch starting with m units runs about m/2 sweeps, building a run of about 3m, which becomes about 3m/2 units: m grows by a factor 3/2 per epoch, exactly m' = 3m/2 + d with a small correction d that depends on the parity of m and on the first items of L. Each epoch takes about 1.5·m2 steps.

sections.heading: A stack driven by parities
html: What happens between the last sweep and the conversion depends on whether m is odd or even, and it changes the first items of the list L. The first item behaves like a small copy of the whole machine: a run that grows by 6 and loses one unit at each odd epoch,
18 u8 → 24 u7 → 30 u6 → 36 u5 → 42 u4 → … → 9 u19 …
and when its units run out it is converted into units itself, taking from the item after it. Deeper items change more and more rarely. Tapes at the start of four epochs:
The right-hand part (4 u^17 4 u^15 4 u^4 4 u^3 4 1) is frozen: new items are pushed on the left faster than old ones are used.

sections.heading: Only past the right end
html: The machine stops only when state F reads a 0. A closed tape language (a finite description of every tape the run can produce, here from windows of 4 cells, checked by Lean) shows that this can only happen when F walks off the right end of the tape. Since the head works at the left end, that needs the whole stack to be used up in one cascade.
Whether that ever happens depends on the sequence of parities of m, which looks random: a Collatz-like question. Nothing seen so far comes close: the stack grows by about one item every three epochs.

sections.heading: How far it was followed, and why a halt looks unlikely
html: With the rule, a program can follow the machine exactly and very far: 100,000 epochs take a minute, and by then the number of steps the real machine would have made has about 35,000 digits. A longer run reached 260,000 epochs (a step count of about 91,500 digits). No halt.

The stack grows by about 0.28 entries per epoch, and each epoch disturbs only its top: one entry in 73% of the epochs, two in 22%, three in 4%, four in 0.27%, five in 0.04%. Reaching one entry deeper is about five times rarer each time, while the stack is by now tens of thousands of entries deep. If the parities of the counter behave like coin flips, as they appear to, the stack is never emptied.

This is not a proof, for the same reason the Collatz problem is open: nobody can rule out a very special run of parities. And such runs exist: the next section shows a list with the real stack that halts, and that no invariant on parities can rule out the halt.

sections.heading: No invariant on run parities
html: The hope was an invariant that looks only at the parities of the runs: a set of parity words (odd/even for each run, in order) that contains the word of the start list [12, 19], that the visit map never leaves, and that holds no word of a halting list. Lean proves that no such set exists (no_parity_invariant), and the same for the runs taken mod 4, mod 8 and mod 16 (no_residue_invariant).

The proof is a chain of lists. Each list has the same residue word as the image of the one before it, so any set of words closed under the map must contain them all, and the last list halts at its next visit. Any invariant on residues alone therefore contains a halting list. Step through a chain below; cells are runs, filled ones odd (small print: the run itself), and the number is the run mod the chosen modulus.

The stack is not enough either. At step 181,429 the real run is at the visit [6, 4, u368, 4, u17, 4, u3, 4, 1]. Keep that stack and replace 368 by the 75-digit number m0 = 41155288665286261693662459474261276833979426164594950575389163897113542655: the exact simulator then runs 247 epochs with m odd, each taking one unit from the first counter of the stack until it is used up, and one epoch with m even, and the machine halts, after a number of steps with 780 binary digits. The same holds for m0 plus any multiple of 2248. So an invariant that decides the machine must tell 368 from m0: it has to follow the counter mod 2248 or finer, which is the arithmetic of the 3/2 map itself.

For the real run, a stretch of 247 odd epochs in a row is as unlikely as 247 heads in a row, and it gets worse: from the stack of step 1.1·108 odd epochs alone do not empty the stack within 106 epochs. That is the heuristic case for no halt, and it is still not a proof.

sections.heading: Does any remainder class halt?
html: A generic test used on the whole family: sample the run whenever the head is in state D reading 1 with only 0s to its left. Read rightwards from the head, the tape is then A Um B, one long periodic block between two short context words A and B. The round to the next sample is computed class by class: for a class (A, U, B, m modulo 1 or 2 (the smallest modulus that works for the context)) six values of m are simulated, and when they agree the round is taken to be an affine map of m. Against the direct run to 3·109 steps the class map is right in all 25 rounds it applies to. It is an observed law, not a proved one.

The orbit. Iterated with exact integers from the event at step 181,384 of the run (A = (empty), U = 10, m = 373, B = 14 (01)18 13 (01)4 13 01): 1,742 rounds without meeting a halting class; m then has 519 bits (about 10312 steps of the machine). 1,742 distinct contexts occur, the longest of 2,729 cells.

Can any class halt? Breadth first from the starting context, with every remainder at every context (whether or not the numbers can really produce that sequence of remainders, and only for m large compared with the contexts): 5,000 contexts expanded, 6,526 found, to depth 23. None of them halts; the search is not complete (the set of contexts keeps growing), and it says nothing about a halt that needs a context as long as the block itself.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.493). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 60,039 cells (42,439 left of the start, 9 right), with a density of 1s of 0.937.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Exact reduced map, proved in Lean (halts_iff): read as runs of 1s, the tape changes between visits of the left end by an explicit map on lists, and the machine halts iff the orbit of [12, 1^9] reaches a list with only even runs; a 3/2 counter whose parities drive a stack of slower counters, no halt in 260,000 epochs (about 10^91568 steps).
family: Collatz-like: 3/2 counter feeding a stack of slower counters (exact visit map on run lists)
